hints: At extreme values of $P$, the particle is in limiting equilibrium where friction reaches its maximum magnitude $F = \mu R$.
Resolve perpendicular to the inclined plane to find the normal reaction: $R = mg\cos 21^\circ = 0.6 \times 10 \times \cos 21^\circ$, and compute $F = 0.3R$.
For the least value of $P$, the particle is on the point of slipping downwards, so friction acts up the plane: resolve parallel to the plane as $P_{\text{least}} + F = mg\sin 21^\circ$.
For the greatest value of $P$, the particle is on the point of slipping upwards, so friction acts down the plane: resolve parallel to the plane as $P_{\text{greatest}} - F = mg\sin 21^\circ$.
walkthrough:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane to find the normal reaction force $R$:
$$R = mg\cos 21^\circ = 0.6 \times 10 \times \cos 21^\circ = 6\cos 21^\circ \approx 5.6014\text{ N}$$

Calculate the limiting friction force using $F = \mu R$ with $\mu = 0.3$:
$$F = \mu R = 0.3 \times 6\cos 21^\circ = 1.8\cos 21^\circ \approx 1.6804\text{ N}$$

Calculate the downslope component of the weight:
$$W_{\text{parallel}} = mg\sin 21^\circ = 0.6 \times 10 \times \sin 21^\circ = 6\sin 21^\circ \approx 2.1503\text{ N}$$

For the least value of $P$, the particle is on the point of sliding down the plane, so friction acts up the plane to prevent motion:
$$P_{\text{least}} + F = mg\sin 21^\circ \implies P_{\text{least}} = 6\sin 21^\circ - 1.8\cos 21^\circ \approx 2.1503 - 1.6804 = 0.4699 \approx 0.470\text{ N}$$

For the greatest value of $P$, the particle is on the point of sliding up the plane, so friction acts down the plane:
$$P_{\text{greatest}} - F = mg\sin 21^\circ \implies P_{\text{greatest}} = 6\sin 21^\circ + 1.8\cos 21^\circ \approx 2.1503 + 1.6804 = 3.8307 \approx 3.83\text{ N}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Name the foundational principle: in limiting equilibrium, the friction force reaches its maximum possible value given by the limiting friction law:
$$F = \mu R$$

Write the equation for the normal reaction force $R$ by resolving forces perpendicular to the inclined plane:
$$R = mg\cos\theta$$

Substitute the mass $m = 0.6\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$, and angle $\theta = 21^\circ$:
$$R = 0.6 \times 10 \times \cos 21^\circ = 6\cos 21^\circ \approx 6 \times 0.933580 = 5.60148\text{ N}$$

Multiply the normal reaction by the coefficient of friction $\mu = 0.3$ to find the limiting friction force $F$:
$$F = 0.3 \times 5.60148 = 1.68044\text{ N}$$

Calculate the component of the particle's weight acting down the line of greatest slope:
$$W_{\text{slope}} = mg\sin\theta = 0.6 \times 10 \times \sin 21^\circ = 6\sin 21^\circ \approx 6 \times 0.358368 = 2.15021\text{ N}$$

Consider the case of the least force $P$. When $P$ is at its minimum, the particle is on the verge of sliding down the plane, so friction $F$ acts up the plane to oppose impending motion:
$$P_{\text{least}} + F = mg\sin 21^\circ$$

Rearrange to solve for $P_{\text{least}}$ by subtracting $F$ from both sides:
$$P_{\text{least}} = mg\sin 21^\circ - F = 2.15021 - 1.68044 = 0.46977\text{ N} \approx 0.470\text{ N} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

Now consider the greatest force $P$. When $P$ is at its maximum, the particle is on the verge of sliding up the plane, so friction $F$ acts down the plane:
$$P_{\text{greatest}} - F = mg\sin 21^\circ$$

Rearrange to solve for $P_{\text{greatest}}$ by adding $F$ to both sides:
$$P_{\text{greatest}} = mg\sin 21^\circ + F = 2.15021 + 1.68044 = 3.83065\text{ N} \approx 3.83\text{ N} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$
